newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt rights groups, opposition slam emergency law.
newsitem.headline: Egypt rights groups, opposition slam emergency law.

text.p: Human rights groups and opposition parties on Tuesday slammed the Egyptian parliament's decision to extend emergency law into the next century, with many saying the law had increased the political violence it was meant to combat.

The 444-seat house on Sunday approved a presidential decree to extend for three more years the emergency law, which has been in force since Moslem militant army officers assassinated president Anwar Sadat on October 6, 1981.

The government has said in the past it wants to extend the law, which gives security forces broad powers of arrest and detention, to combat militant groups bent on overthrowing it and setting up a strict Islamic state.

But for the current extension it has also pointed to its expanding economy. Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri, who has engineered a successful privatisation programme, said the aim was to protect the economy from sabotage by "terrorists".
But an editorial in the opposition al-Wafd party newspaper said the law would harm rather than protect that economy.

"Emergency law is against investment. It is simply a law which means that the situation is not safe and therefore any investor will think a thousand times before working in an unsafe country," the editorial said.
"Those who approved the extension of emergency law have presented the best gift to Egypt's enemy," it added.
Mostafa Kamel Murad, head of the opposition Ahrar party, said the extension of the emergency law highlighted the weakness of the government in quashing Moslem militant violence.
"A strong government does not need emergency law, but a weak, shaky government resorts to this law and applies it out of context," Murad said in his column in the party's daily paper.

"If they say terrorism is the reason, it would have been better to apply emergency law in the (southern) provinces where some terrorist incidents are found. But we can never agree to have it imposed on the republic of Egypt," he added.

Militants staged daring attacks in the capital in 1993, attempting to assassinate the former prime minister and two of his ministers. Between 1992 and 1994 they also killed a secular writer and several tourists in attacks that damaged the Egyptian tourism industry at the time.

But bloody police crackdowns and the use of military courts to issue swift sentences have curbed militant violence in the capital Cairo over the past few years, confining most militant attacks to the southern provinces.

In a notable exception militants massacred 18 Greek tourists outside a Cairo hotel last April. The Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group) claimed repsonsibility, saying it thought the tourists were Israelis.

"Emergency law has over the past few years been turned into a tool in the hands of the authorities allowing them to ignore many rights and basic freedoms guaranteed by the constitution and international conventions," said the independent Egyptian Organisation for Human Rights (EOHR).

As an example, it said military courts had issued 74 death sentences since President Hosni Mubarak approved their use to try militants in 1992. Supreme Emergency State Security courts, which fall under the jurisdiction of emergency law, sentenced 10 militants to death between 1996-97, EOHR said.

"What is sure is that violence has escalated markedly over the past few years under the state of emergency. The state of emergency has not prevented assassination and attempts on the lives and property of government officials, citizens, writers and tourists," said two other human rights groups.

The groups, the independent Centre for Human Rights Legal Aid and al-Nadim Centre for the Management and Rehabilitation, said in a joint statement that security measures alone could not curb political violence and urged the government to deal with the political, social and economic problems that caused such violence.
